name: Sodium oxybate (GHB)
lead: Sodium oxybate is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a central nervous system depressant. As a prescription product it is approved in the US for cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy, and in lower-sodium form for idiopathic hypersomnia [1][2][3]. Outside medical use GHB is a controlled drug in most countries [4].

In appearance and physique circles it has been discussed because of its effect on slow-wave sleep. The reasoning is a chain: deeper sleep, which proponents associate with a night-time growth hormone release and better recovery, which would support harder training and more muscle and a leaner physique [5]. GHB was in fact sold in the US as a dietary supplement to bodybuilders in 1990 for weight control and sleep, until the FDA warned in November of that year that its sale was illegal [4].

Published trials evaluate sodium oxybate for narcolepsy, idiopathic hypersomnia and other sleep or neurological conditions rather than for looks [6][7][8]. The US label carries a boxed warning for CNS depression and for abuse and misuse [2].

chain: Proponents link slow-wave sleep with growth hormone release and recovery
Better recovery is claimed to support training and a leaner, more muscular look
angle.text: Bodybuilding forum users have described GHB as a sleep enhancer and growth hormone booster, with better workouts the hoped-for payoff. The drug itself is a tightly controlled prescription product for sleep disorders, and no trial has tested it for appearance.

infobox: Rx-only with restricted distribution; US Schedule III as a medicine, GHB itself Schedule I [4]

paras: Grokipedia reports FDA approval for cataplexy in narcolepsy on 17 July 2002 and for excessive daytime sleepiness in 2005 [1]. Current labeling for Lumryz covers cataplexy or excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy from age 7 [2]. A lower-sodium formulation is approved for idiopathic hypersomnia [1][9]. Clinical guidelines on narcolepsy and central hypersomnolence include sodium oxybate [10][11][12].

In Italy and Austria it has also been approved for alcohol dependence and withdrawal, and reviews describe it as one of several agents in alcohol use disorder [4][13]. Research has additionally looked at cluster headache, laryngeal dystonia, Parkinson disease sleep problems and postoperative delirium [14][15][16].

The GHB family of compounds was described by Alexander Zaytsev in 1874. French researcher Henri Laborit studied GHB as a GABA analogue in the early 1960s, and it was marketed in Europe from 1964 as an intravenous anaesthetic [4]. Italy approved it for alcohol withdrawal in 1991 [4].

In May 1990 GHB was sold in the US as a dietary supplement aimed at bodybuilders for weight control and as a sleep aid, and the FDA warned in November 1990 that its sale was illegal; illicit club use followed [4]. Orphan Medical ran narcolepsy trials in the 1990s, the FDA approved Xyrem in 2002 with a risk-management programme, and Jazz Pharmaceuticals acquired Orphan Medical in 2005 [4]. A once-nightly extended-release product, Lumryz, was approved in 2023 [4].

GHB is an endogenous metabolite of GABA that acts at GABA-B receptors and at specific GHB receptors; the full mechanism is described as incompletely understood [1][4]. In narcolepsy treatment it increases slow-wave sleep and is thought to make sleep more restorative [1][4]. A study using sodium oxybate to manipulate sleep spindles examined their causal role in memory consolidation [17], and a Washington University study used it to increase slow-wave sleep while sampling cerebrospinal fluid amyloid-beta [18].
A review of GHB pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and toxicology covers its short-chain fatty acid chemistry, its therapeutic uses and its use as a recreational and chemsex drug [19].

The label's boxed warning covers CNS depression, including clinically significant respiratory depression and obtundation at recommended amounts, and abuse and misuse [2]. It also lists sleep-disordered breathing, depression and suicidality, and behavioral or psychiatric reactions [2]. Wikipedia lists dizziness, nausea and headache as the most common adverse effects, and reports that overdose, especially with alcohol or other depressants, can cause respiratory depression, coma and death [4]. Grokipedia reports that illicit GHB has been misused in drug-facilitated crimes [1].

Because of these risks, sodium oxybate is distributed under restricted programs. In 2007 Jazz and Orphan Medical pleaded guilty to felony misbranding related to off-label marketing and paid $20 million in total [4].

The US Hillory J. Farias and Samantha Reid Date-Rape Prevention Act of 2000 placed GHB in Schedule I while sodium oxybate under an FDA application is Schedule III for medical use [4]. Status elsewhere includes Schedule 2 in the UK and Schedule 8 in Australia [4]. Brands include Xyrem, Xywav, Lumryz, Alcover (Italy) and Gamma-OH (France) [4].
In bodybuilding forums GHB has appeared in discussions of sleep enhancers and growth hormone boosters [5][20].

A multicenter randomized placebo-controlled trial and a later 2006 study with 200-plus narcolepsy participants evaluated sodium oxybate with and without modafinil, reporting improvements in cataplexy and daytime sleepiness [6][7]. A phase 3 randomised withdrawal trial supported low-sodium oxybate in idiopathic hypersomnia [8][21]. Registered studies include a 60-participant trial on enhancing slow-wave sleep [22] and a 25-participant exploratory study of endocrine changes in narcolepsy patients [23]. No studies were found testing sodium oxybate for appearance.

lore.intro: On T Nation, GHB under the Xyrem name was discussed in a 2008 thread as a sleep enhancer and growth hormone secretagogue [20].

claims.claim: GHB boosts growth hormone for recovery and leanness
claims.believers: The thread's original poster quoted a bodybuilding-supplement author calling GHB a strong growth hormone secretagogue without the risks of injected GH, and one user reported a shaky post-training sensation and good recovery [20].
claims.experts: The thread contains no hormone measurements. Slow-wave sleep enhancement is documented in narcolepsy treatment [1]; an exploratory endocrine study in narcolepsy patients was registered [23].

claims.claim: It deepens sleep and improves workouts
claims.believers: One user recalled excellent sleep, better workouts and no aches, while another slept 7-8 hours but woke unrefreshed [20].
claims.experts: Trials show improved sleepiness and cataplexy in narcolepsy and that the drug increases slow-wave sleep [6][7][1]; no trial tested athletic outcomes.

claims.claim: GHB can be used safely as a sleep aid
claims.believers: Commenters have described it as a milder alternative to other sedatives, while some in the same thread warned of addiction [20].
claims.experts: The FDA label carries a boxed warning for CNS depression, abuse and misuse [2].

card.summary: A narcolepsy prescription drug that is chemically GHB; approved for sleep disorders, untested for looks, and tightly controlled for serious safety reasons.
card.note: Boxed warning for CNS depression and abuse; restricted distribution and controlled-substance status.

quick.overview:
Sodium oxybate is the prescription form of GHB, approved in the US for cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy. It is tightly controlled.

It appears in recovery and sleep discussions because it deepens slow-wave sleep. No trial has tested it for appearance outcomes, and the wiki found no community threads to cite.
quick.mechanism: It acts at GABA-B receptors and GHB-specific receptors, depressing the central nervous system and increasing slow-wave sleep.
quick.risks: The label boxed warning covers CNS and respiratory depression and abuse or misuse. Reference sources report overdose risk, especially with alcohol or sedatives. It is a controlled substance, with restricted distribution as a medicine.
